title: Plant a pepper seedling's root plug in a planter box, backfilled level on every side and firmed so it stands alone
instruction: Plant the seedling in the planter box, level with the soil, and firm it in so it stands by itself.
context: Planting is a core task of landscaping and groundskeeping workers (O*NET 37-3011.00, about 1.19 million US jobs: "Plant seeds, bulbs, foliage, flowering plants, grass, ground covers, trees, or shrubs"), and home gardeners set out seedlings each spring. The hole is dug about twice as wide as the root plug, so the plug does not stay put: soil pushed in from one side shoves it over. One hand holds it upright by the root ball (never by the stem) while the other works the dug soil back in round it. The soil must reach the plug's top on every side, the plug neither buried nor proud, and be firmed so the seedling stands when let go. An air pocket on one side leaves it leaning, and a creased stem or a crushed leaf sets the plant back or kills it. Watering in comes next and is not part of the task.
setup: Positions are in cm, measured forward (x) from the line between the two arm bases and to the robot's left (y) from the midpoint between them; heights are above the table top. (1) Planter box: a wooden planter box, 30 x 30 cm inside and 9 cm deep, centered at x 28.0, y 0.0, fixed. It is filled with moist peat-perlite potting mix, firmed level 1 cm under its top edge (8 cm above the table). A planting hole 10.4 cm across and 6.2 cm deep is dug in its middle, as with a trowel (for repeatable trials, with a round former that stops at that depth). (2) Loose mix: the mix dug out of the hole, 440 mL (200 g), crumbled into lumps and heaped round the hole from 6 to 10 cm out, up to 2.3 cm high. The gap round a level plug is about 360 mL, so the loose mix is about 1.2 times its volume; in the simulator 105 of the 200 clods fill it to the surface. (3) Seedling: a sweet pepper transplant grown in a 3601 (36-cell) insert, popped out of its cell with its root ball whole: 4.9 x 5.7 cm across the top, tapering to 3.6 x 4.4 cm at the bottom, 5.7 cm deep (118 mL), 70 g moist. Its stem is 3.6 mm across and 9 cm tall above the plug, springy (stiff at the base, soft near the tip), ending in a growing tip. Two narrow seed leaves (1.8 cm) sit 2 cm up it. Above them are four simple, oval true leaves on springy stalks, all toward the robot's right: three 5-6.5 cm long (blade up to 2.6 cm wide) 3.2-4.2 cm up, and a young 2.5 cm one 7 cm up. The stem and leaves weigh about 5.5 g. It stands upright on the bench beside the box at x 22.0, y 26.0, its 4.9 cm sides facing the robot and away. The layout is the same in every trial.
scoring: Measured at the end, after the plug has been let go (every gripper at least 1 cm clear of it). The soil level on a side of the plug is the height the backfill reaches in that side's quarter of the gap. The trial scores 1.0 when the plug is in the hole within 10 degrees of upright, its top within 1 cm of the firmed surface (not buried, not proud), the soil reaches within 1 cm of the plug's top on all four sides, at least 85% of the hole round it is filled, at most 10% of the loose mix is spilled out of the planter box, and it is firm: after it has stood still for 1 s, a 0.5 N side push 5 cm above the plug's top, 1 s each way, turns it less than 5 degrees. It scores 0.75 when all of that holds but it is not firm. It scores 0.5 when the plug is within 20 degrees of upright, three sides are filled to within 1 cm of its top, at least 60% of the hole is filled, and it has been let go. It scores 0.25 when the plug is in the hole within 20 degrees of upright with at least 40% of the hole filled. More than 10% of the mix spilled caps the score at 0.5. The whole trial scores 0 if the seedling is damaged: the stem bent more than 45 degrees at either joint of the model (its base or mid-height), or the stem or a leaf squeezed between the two fingers of one hand (either for 2 control steps running). Otherwise it scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Doing nothing scores 0. Why these numbers: 1 cm is the depth gardeners allow for planting a pepper at the soil line it grew at (deeper rots the stem, proud dries the plug); 10 degrees is a lean you see at a glance; 0.5 N is a light breeze or a watering-can stream on the stem, which a firmed seedling shrugs off; 45 degrees within 4.5 cm of a 3.6 mm stem stretches its surface about 3%, a sharp bend taken to crease it (an estimate, not a measured kink angle). Real trial: mark the four sides on the soil with plant labels; measure the soil level against the plug's top at each mark with a steel rule; read the tilt with a phone inclinometer on a 15 cm bamboo skewer pushed into the plug's center before the trial; push with a 1 N spring gauge (0.01 N divisions) 5 cm above the plug's top, each way; weigh the spilled mix, and the loose mix left outside the hole (200 g minus both went in). Damage: photograph the seedling before and after; a creased, kinked or broken stem, or a crushed or torn leaf, scores 0.
reset_notes: Lift the plant out, scoop the backfill and the loose mix into a tub, re-dig the hole with the former to its depth stop, heap 200 g of loose mix round it by weight, and use a fresh plug from the same tray.
fidelity: Real size and mass (plug 70 g, shoot 5.5 g). The stem is two springy segments, stiffness from beam bending with E measured along young tomato stems (Coutand & Moulia 2000). Leaves are flat plates, all on one side: the lower ones swing and fold on springy stalks, the top one only folds, the seed leaves are rigid. The 45 degree kink limit is derived from about 3% surface strain, not measured. Loose mix is 200 rigid 1.1 cm clods that cannot compact. The side push acts at the root ball.
